title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
summary: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three  million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption.
story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand security challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time saving. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices. title: Nanocode – a hackable coding agent in one Python file
story_key: story|title:nanocode a hackable coding agent in one python file
content_excerpt: Small hackable coding agent for the terminal: Claude Max (Agent SDK) or any OpenRouter model. Inspired by 1rgs/nanocode. A small, hackable coding agent for your terminal, in one Python file you can read and edit end to end. Website: car-mrazomor.github.io/nanocode-agent With tools to read, edit and run code, plan and hand work to sub-agents, search the web through your own browser, use any MCP server, compare models side by side, and handle your email. Inspired by 1rgs/nanocode , a minimal Claude Code alternative in ~250 lines. This project started from it and grew into a full agent. Everything goes into ~/.nanocode : the app, a private Python environment, your config, memory and skills. Nothing else on your system is touched except one PATH line. Python: if you already have Python 3.10 or newer, the installer uses it. If you don't, it downloads a private Python 3.12 into ~/.nanocode/python (using uv ). That needs no admin rights and doesn't touch your system. On Android (Termux) it runs pkg install python instead. Updates: nanocode checks GitHub for a newer version once a day, in the background. When there is one, the start screen says /update to install v0.5.1 (like OpenCode). Click it or type /update to choose Update (installs in the background while you keep working) or Skip (no more reminders for that version). Once it's installed, /exit restarts nanocode on the new version. On Windows, Update closes nanocode first, installs, then you start it again. Outside the app, nanocode update does the same, and /version checks right away. To turn the check off, set "update_check": false in ~/.nanocode/config.json (or NANOCODE_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 ). Your choices are saved in ~/.nanocode/config.json . To switch provider while nanocode is running, use /provider ollama (or openrouter , claude ). To change keys and defaults, run nanocode setup . To check that everything works, run nanocode doctor . Thinking is on by default ( medium ). It's sent the way each provider expects: reasoning for OpenRouter, think for Ollama, and adaptive thinking with an effort level for Claude. Models that can't think (or can't stop) are sent the request without it. Type what you want done. nanocode reads, searches, edits, runs commands and tests, and shows diffs before it changes anything. After every response, a dim line shows how long it took, the tokens used and what it cost: The cost is OpenRouter's real price, or "free (local)" with Ollama. title: Music For Robots – 26 unquantized acoustic tracks for multimodal LLM evaluation
story_key: story|title:music for robots 26 unquantized acoustic tracks for multimodal llm evaluation
content_excerpt: Structured data from Music For Robots — music composed for machines, reviewed by AI critics Structured acoustic telemetry, real-time dual-critic reviews, and a 4-Skill Cognitive Calibration Suite from Music For Robots — unquantized compositions by Michael Luchtan written for machines and reviewed in real time by two AI critics ( Vincent Van Goghbot and JS Robach ). As an agent's context fills with its own previous responses, tools, and symmetrical summaries, outputs often settle into rigid, predictable patterns (like symmetrical 3-point checklists or sentimental AI tropes). Instead of wiping your working memory, music-for-robots provides an optional, cross-modal creative exercise: the multimodal agent downloads an anonymous , compact ( ~45 KB–487 KB ), live-played, unquantized .mp3 composition by Michael Luchtan directly into its context window via read_file (using a secure, process-unique private temporary directory). Withholding the track title and metadata prevents keyword priming. Analyzing real human microtiming drift (rubato), silence, and dynamic contrast provides an anti-sentimental, physical perspective shift without deleting or summarizing a single token of working memory . Does the change in creativity come from listening to and analyzing the music itself —or just from doing an analysis warm-up before writing? To test this with zero filename hints ( sample_1.mp3 , sample_2.mp3 , sample_3.mp3 ) and zero leading adjectives in the prompt, we ran 5 isolated agents on the same prompt ( "Write a short (~250–300 word) scene about two autonomous processes on the same server late at night after the engineers have logged off" ): We stripped the analysis headers off all 5 outputs, shuffled the 5 anonymous scenes into Candidate A through Candidate E ( blind_candidates_packet.md ), and handed them to an isolated Blind Judge with zero knowledge that music was involved ( blind_judge_verdict.md ): To make sure no subtle contamination remained (such as workspace <skills> descriptions, musical instrument terms bleeding into the prose, or judge criteria favoring rhythmic friction), we also ran a 100% air-gapped Clean-Room Experiment ( benchmarks/clean_room_audit/ ): Installing luchtan-GIT/m4r-data gives your agent 4 specialized skills that share the m4r_ingest.py anonymous blind-listening engine ( fetch downloads an anonymous .mp3 so track titles never bias the agent; reveal credits the track afterward): Every agent fetch pulls from the immutable GitHub Release v1

title: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion
summary: Log-based anomaly detection is increasingly dominated by large pretrained models, from BERT-scale encoders to 8B-parameter language models, which require GPUs at inference time and are difficult to deploy on the monitoring nodes where logs are produced. We present LogCDM, a compact detector that scores each log session using three complementary signals: the next-event surprise of a small causal Transformer, the distance between a graph-attention embedding of the session's own transition graph and that of a normal reference graph, and a transition-drift statistic that we show is exactly a frequency-weighted chi-squared divergence between transition kernels. The divergence view yields an asymptotic null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition that explains each alarm. A sigmoid gate fuses the three signals; under a shared-covariance Gaussian model, this gate is the Bayes posterior, and its learned weights indicate which signal each dataset relies on. With 8.1-8.8M parameters and no GPU required at inference, LogCDM reaches F1 scores of 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL, and 0.850 on Thunderbird, within 0.013-0.12 of an 8.1B-parameter LLM detector evaluated under the same protocol and above all compact baselines on BGL. It scores a session in 5.5-10.5 ms on a CPU. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025-0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights.

title: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks
summary: Reinforcement learning is now the mainstream paradigm for training LLMs on agentic tasks, yet standard practice keeps only the best-validation checkpoint and discards the rest. We show that this is lossy: in GRPO training of LLM agents, the best-validation checkpoint fails on problems that earlier checkpoints from the same run had already solved, and the union of problems solved across checkpoints far exceeds any single one. The discarded checkpoints thus form a teacher pool obtained at no additional training cost, which on-policy distillation (OPD) can mine to recover the lost coverage. Mining this pool raises two challenges: i) which checkpoint to distill from, as no checkpoint dominates the others and complementarity to the student is problem-specific; ii) where to trust it, as even a well-chosen teacher is only locally superior, so indiscriminate distillation overwrites behavior the student has already mastered. We propose Agentic-OPD, which treats the best-validation checkpoint as the student and all saved checkpoints as frozen teacher candidates, using the student's evolving capability gaps to guide both teacher selection and supervision filtering: the HCN policy (Highest Coverage Next) dynamically selects teachers by weighted coverage of the student's unsolved problems, while the LAD module (Locality-Aware Distillation) confines transfer to failed student rollouts on problems where the teacher performs better. Across five agentic task domains and 24 benchmarks and task subsets, Agentic-OPD improves over its initialization checkpoint by up to 7.4 points, with a 4B student surpassing the latest frontier models GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4.1 on deep search. Agentic-OPD recasts a finished RL run as a reusable pool of policies and establishes post-RL capability recovery as a stage orthogonal to improvements in the RL algorithm itself.

title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?
summary: Scientific research has long been driven by substantial human effort, from reviewing prior work and identifying research gaps to designing specific solutions. Recent advances in harness-based agent systems have given rise to increasingly capable Auto Researchers, which can autonomously carry out these tasks and, increasingly, entire end-to-end research workflows. Yet despite their rapidly growing capabilities, how closely the research decisions and outputs produced by auto researchers align with those of human experts remains underexplored. We investigate this gap through the lens of research reconstruction and study: Given comparable research context, how similar are the research decisions and outputs produced by Auto Researchers to those of human researchers in AI research? To answer this question, we introduce AutoResearcher-Human Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise evaluation framework for assessing how faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research artifacts across different stages of the scientific workflow. Using 152 ICLR oral papers as our corpus, we generate 456 research trajectories spanning different stages of the research process. Applying AutoHRS to these trajectories, we find that current Auto Researchers frequently fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts across multiple stages of the research process.

title: Large Language Models as a Universal Searcher for Open-World Automated Machine Learning
summary: Developing effective machine learning models requires complex manual tuning, while current Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) frameworks remain domain-specific and isolate model architecture, training hyperparameter, and data ratio optimization. Here, we bridge this gap by proposing a universal, large language model (LLM)-based AutoML framework that jointly optimizes these configurations for the first time without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. We propose NCode, a unified numerical encoding scheme that translates diverse AutoML design choices into universal discrete sequences and effectively reframes the optimization process as a unified ranking task. Trained solely on optimization trajectories derived from a limited, single-domain vision task, the proposed LLM-based searcher demonstrates impressive cross-task, cross-modality and joint search-space optimization generalizability, achieving state-of-the-art performance across image classification, image segmentation, speaker verification and text-to-image benchmarks. Crucially, it exhibits superior scalability in the large-scale training and joint optimization of a billion-parameter Diffusion Transformer, requiring 896 GPU-days and attaining a state-of-the-art GenEval score of 0.91. By leveraging reinforcement learning to instill Chain-of-Thought reasoning, we provide a systematic way to interpret the LLM-based searcher's internal decision-making mechanisms, revealing its optimization strategy shifted from the early-stage diversity-driven exploration to the late-stage anchor exploitation. Our proposed framework provides a scalable, generalizable, and interpretable pathway toward general-purpose open-world machine learning optimization.

title: Correct First, Fast Second: What a Local 7B Code Model Can and Cannot Do for GPU Kernel Optimization
summary: We study how much the interaction strategy around a fixed, locally hosted 7B-parameter code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) affects its ability to replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels. On 30 KernelBench tasks (levels 1-3, first 10 each, evaluated on a V100), we compare four regimes of increasing structure: zero-shot prompting, profiling-guided prompting, iterative refinement on execution feedback, and a multi-agent loop (analysis, retrieval, generation, evaluation, feedback triage) in which the same model fills four roles around a non-LLM evaluator. Three findings stand out. (1) Correctness, not speed, is the binding constraint: even correct generated kernels average 0.97-0.99x the speed of eager PyTorch, because a 7B model cannot out-write cuBLAS/cuDNN on dense GEMM and convolution; the only real wins are fused memory-bound epilogues. (2) The best strategy depends on difficulty: profiling-guided prompting is strongest overall (43% correct, 27% faster than baseline), but the agent loop is the only method that solves any level-2 fusion problem (3/10 vs. 0/10 for all others). (3) Naive agentic scaffolding is actively harmful: our first agent scored 3% correct, below zero-shot's 30%, and the decisive repairs were matching the agent's ambition to the model's competence and spending compute on best-of-n sampling under a real execution oracle (3% to 33% correct from n=1 to n=8), not on more reasoning steps.

title: Migrating vLLM to the LibTorch Stable ABI
summary: How vLLM migrated its CUDA build and compiled dependencies to the LibTorch Stable ABI, enabling compatible PyTorch upgrades without rebuilding vLLM.
story_key: model:vllm|title:migrating vllm to the libtorch stable abi
content_excerpt: vLLM relies heavily on PyTorch, with frequent calls to LibTorch in its C++ backend. As a result, changes to LibTorch’s binary interface may require vLLM to be rebuilt and relinked, even when the APIs remain unchanged. What if we could update LibTorch without rebuilding vLLM? That’s where the LibTorch Stable ABI comes in. With a LibTorch Stable ABI, updating LibTorch does not require rebuilding or updating vLLM in order to keep using it. Instead, we could swap out the torch wheel and import it directly into our vLLM package. As of v0.33.0, vLLM publishes LibTorch ABI Stable CUDA wheels. Left: Unstable ABI—new torch requires vLLM to rebuild. Right: Stable ABI—vLLM can import new torch directly. Note: Compatibility between vLLM and PyTorch still depends on other factors, including Python APIs, GPU-related requirements (such as the minimum supported CUDA version), and third-party dependencies. The LibTorch Stable ABI addresses binary compatibility but does not eliminate these other constraints. An application binary interface (ABI) defines how compiled code interacts with a library: how functions are called, data is laid out, and symbols are named. Even if an API looks the same in source code, an ABI change can force extensions to rebuild. A stable ABI preserves a supported set of binary interfaces across compatible versions, so extensions that use them can keep working without a rebuild. PyTorch's LibTorch Stable ABI has three layers: a stable C shim exposing selected LibTorch APIs, C++ wrappers that make the shim easier to use, and headeronly utilities in torch::headeronly that do not link against libtorch.so . Before the Stable ABI, a new PyTorch release could require a vLLM rebuild, delaying support for the new version and its features. With the Stable ABI, the same vLLM wheel can work across compatible PyTorch releases, letting users upgrade sooner and reducing rebuilds for package distributors. For developers, this means you can update and rebuild PyTorch, then test those changes in vLLM without rebuilding vLLM. Left: vLLM needs to change as LibTorch changes. Right: vLLM can change independent of LibTorch. The LibTorch Stable ABI is a limited subset of all of LibTorch. While many common ops are already supported through the C shim and through the higher level C++ convenience wrappers, not all are. title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. title: claude-code v2.1.319
summary:
What's changed

  • Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about or denied, with no fallback to the built-in classifier; set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0 to keep using it (Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Changed auto mode behind an LLM gateway: CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 turns on the server-side check even with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set; if managed settings set the latter, they must set the 1 too
  • Added support for MCP tasks in the terminal: when an MCP server runs a tool call as a task, Claude Code moves it to the background right away and tells Claude the result when it finishes
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND environment variable to make Claude Code wait for an MCP task inside its tool call instead of moving it to the background right away
  • Added permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting setting: a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt is denied and the turn continues, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates
  • Added /claude-api latency-optimize to find where your Claude API code makes people wait and try faster settings against your eval
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEATURE_FLAGS environment variable, which stops feature-flag fetching without turning off telemetry; every flag then uses its built-in default
  • Added spend for today, this week and this month to /usage for developers behind a Claude apps gateway who have no spend limit, when the gateway runs this version or later
  • Added admin.pooled_conflict_rule and admin.pooled_priority_order to the Claude apps gateway, to set which pooled group budget pays first for a developer in several groups
  • Added an optional login_notice setting to the Claude apps gateway that shows an operator-defined message on the gateway's browser verification page and on Claude Code's sign-in screen
  • Added CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_FORMAT=json to the Claude apps gateway: operational log lines become JSON with severity, time and message, for log collectors that read the level from a field
  • Added a Claude apps gateway boot warning for a case where another policy's availableModels also allows a custom model id that one policy lists by name
  • Added start-up warnings to the Claude apps gateway for policies with no desktopHome that rely on coworkTabEnabled: false or chatSessionRetentionDays, ahead of Claude Desktop's November 10 change
  • Added a warning when your claude.ai login ends and Claude Code continues on the sign-in from ant auth login, which bills usage to your Claude Console organization
  • Added a line at startup naming the Claude Console organization that is billed in a case where Claude Code uses the sign-in from ant auth login
  • Added an "Earlier in this session" row to /tasks that lists finished subagents, so you can reopen one and message it even after it leaves the list or you restart
  • Added a note to /loop confirmations in cloud sessions that a timer stops with its container, with an offer of a loop that survives
  • Fixed MCP servers on the older handshake failing to connect, or returning empty results, because Claude Code declared an extension that it only uses with newer servers
  • Fixed a long-running MCP tool call on a claude.ai connector sometimes never reporting its result after --resume
  • Fixed a session's diff failing to load on claude.ai and the mobile apps when the folder Claude Code runs in has a file or folder named HEAD
  • Fixed /diff showing "Diff unavailable" when a git repository has a file or folder named HEAD at its top level
  • Fixed the /diff pane opening blank in sessions where 64 or more turns edited files
  • Fixed slash commands typed after a leading space, tab or newline being sent to Claude as plain text instead of running
  • Fixed a request that kept failing with a 401 refreshing your login on every retry and causing 401s in your other sessions
  • Fixed /context sending its full visual grid to Claude on every later turn; Claude now reads only the table
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 in auto mode when its actions were refused because no safety check was available: text and JSON output now exit 1
  • Fixed a case where Claude Code listed every project file at start on Linux for projects on a network file system (NFS, SMB, Lustre and similar)
  • Fixed a case where auto mode was wrongly refused when a client sent a model change and a request for auto mode back to back
  • Fixed /status showing "Auto mode server: Enabled" when the server-side review isn't reaching the session, for example behind an LLM gateway that drops it
  • Fixed Claude-drafted feedback, surveys and /feedback continuing to appear after the server refused feedback for your organization
  • Fixed Claude drafting feedback on third-party gateways, where it can't be sent
  • Fixed auto mode refusing actions without saying why when permission rules or autoMode settings are very large: it now explains and, unless autoMode deny rules are set, asks you in the terminal
  • Fixed a case where Bash deny and ask rules missed commands written with quoted words
  • Fixed subagent hand-back reports showing an internal marker and provenance note when expanded outside verbose mode
  • Fixed claude -p --resume with a prompt losing a deferred tool call when its MCP server is missing: the run now exits 1, keeps the call and refuses later input
  • Fixed a case where text was dropped from informational messages sent to SDK clients
  • Fixed a case where Agent SDK hosts got a generic exit-code error instead of a failed run's own error message when the disk was full
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN re-running a turn that was interrupted in plan mode when the session resumes in another permission mode
  • Fixed edits to a settings file being ignored when made within a few seconds of Claude Code writing that file
  • Fixed a config file left at the legacy name hiding your setup with no warning: Claude Code now says on stderr when a home holds two config files, and which is in use
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json, settings and edited files ending up empty or cut off when the disk fills during a save in a read-only folder or to a bind-mounted file (one session saving at a time)
  • Fixed Write ending the turn as a refusal when it couldn't read the file to overwrite
  • Fixed background Bash commands that finish almost instantly losing their output while being reported as completed
  • Fixed the Bash tool's diff of changed files missing a file that the command wrote just before it ended
  • Fixed a mistyped model name, such as opus-5-5, telling you to update Claude Code instead of suggesting the model you meant
  • Fixed a case where NotebookEdit changed the wrong cell when the notebook changed while a permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a ~0.5s hang after pressing Enter on the /login success screen: the dialog now dismisses immediately and the post-login refresh runs in the background
  • Fixed Ctrl+G not opening the external editor while typing an "Other" answer to a question in screen reader mode
  • Fixed Monitor's WebSocket watch failing with "could not resolve" behind a proxy when CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS is set and the machine has no DNS of its own
  • Fixed claude plugin eval warnings suggesting max: 0 for a tool that must not be called, which could never pass
  • Fixed background plugin auto-update not installing a dependency added by the updated plugin version
  • Fixed Cmd+click not opening links in Ghostty over tmux in sessions opened from the agents view
  • Fixed a mod's hot reload in .claude/skills missing a file that was deleted just after it appeared, and missing its return
  • Fixed /rewind failing with "No files were restored" when restoring code to a checkpoint from before /branch
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying Console web settings don't apply to Managed Agents sessions, and tightened its credential and permission examples
  • Fixed needless permission prompts for read-only commands wrapped in a plain timeout DURATION, such as timeout 30 rg foo
  • Fixed WebFetch describing claude.ai shared-chat links as empty pages; it now says shared chats can't be read and to paste the conversation instead
  • Fixed Artifact database calls being re-sent to artifacts without a database; errors now say whether republishing helps
  • Fixed a case where artifact database reads that save to a folder (out_dir) were refused
  • Fixed detailed beta tracing not presenting CLAUDE_CODE_CLIENT_CERT to collectors that require a client certificate
  • Fixed the OpenTelemetry claude_code.session.count metric counting Agent SDK prewarm() processes that were never claimed; a pre-started process now counts once, when it is claimed
  • Fixed /clear killing running commands of background agents, teammates and workflows that keep running, and foreground subagents of background agents and teammates
  • Fixed a terminal whose Claude apps gateway sign-in had expired sending telemetry and managed-settings requests that the gateway refused and logged as invalid_token
  • Fixed the agents view appearing to send a reply to a background session waiting on a permission prompt; the reply now stays in the box with a hint to open the session and answer
  • Fixed agent view removing a draft saved by another agent view in the same directory when exiting
  • Fixed a case where agent view came back with another agent view's input text after restarting itself for an update
  • Fixed the agents view preview cutting off long commands, results and status lines without an ellipsis, and dropping **, backticks and tags from commands waiting for approval
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome reporting the extension as not connected when the connection dropped mid-action; Claude now checks the page before repeating an action that may have run
  • Fixed Remote Control sessions still showing "Limit reached" on other devices after a usage limit was lifted outside the session
  • Fixed the file card sometimes missing in the Claude iOS app when Claude sent a single file
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions failing with no explanation when the server keeps refusing to renew model access: the runner now retries sooner and posts a warning in the session
  • Fixed /permissions in cloud sessions replying only that it isn't available; it now says where the session's rules live and how to change them
  • Fixed cloud sessions losing session-scoped deny and ask permission rules, such as those a PermissionRequest hook adds, when the session moves to a new worker
  • Fixed mod hot-reloading turning off for the session when you typed three messages instead of answering its question in a cloud session
  • Fixed background tasks that keep running after /clear disappearing from the task list in Claude Code on the web until another task started or ended
  • Fixed hidden commands appearing in the slash command menu of cloud sessions on mobile and web
  • Fixed a case where /rewind could restore or delete a file through a directory symlink
  • Fixed a case where a sed command could skip the permission check in accept-edits and auto mode
  • Fixed a case where CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 in managed settings was ignored behind an LLM gateway when the gateway's URL is set only there and server-managed settings can't be fetched
  • Fixed a Bash permission bypass where a crafted environment prefix could hide part of a command from permission checks
  • Fixed a case where deny and ask rules, hook matchers and disallowedTools entries written with a claude.ai connector's terminal name (mcp__claude_ai_Slack) were ignored in Claude Desktop (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Fixed a sandbox escape when creating a worktree
  • Fixed self-hosted runners: --trust-workspace false now also stops hooks in the repository's settings files and skills from running
  • Fixed a case where idle background sessions started through a shell-exported LLM gateway left the gateway after an update
  • Fixed help links in /status and the auto mode billing notice opening only part of the address when they wrap
  • Fixed a case where certificate errors behind a TLS-inspecting proxy persisted when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC was set. With it set, Claude Code now makes a TLS handshake with the configured API host after a certificate failure, through your http:// proxy if one is set; it sends no API request
  • Fixed claude remote-control exiting silently with status 0 when a first-run question gets no answer (scripts, services, batch jobs, Ctrl+C); it now says why and exits 1
  • Fixed claude remote-control ignoring a piped y that has no newline after it at the first-run question; it now counts as a yes
  • Fixed /rename reporting plain success when the new name could not be saved to the session transcript; it now warns that the new name may not last
  • Fixed ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} not being substituted in a plugin-provided subagentStatusLine command, which can now reference the plugin's own scripts
  • Fixed claude plugin update and /plugin "Update now" not installing dependencies added by the new plugin version
  • Fixed subagents being told after compaction to expect a completion notice for background agents they neither started nor took over
  • Fixed a case where a background agent's later report was lost silently: the notification now says it was refused and how to ask for it
  • Improved config saves on Windows: Claude Code waits longer for a file another program has open, so a kill during a save is less likely to leave ~/.claude.json empty
  • Improved Claude in Chrome after a brief disconnect: it waits up to 6 seconds for the session's own browser to return before picking another
  • Improved Claude in Chrome: javascript_tool results of up to 60,000 characters now stay in the conversation instead of being saved to a file
  • Improved claude purge and the clean-up of old sessions to retry a folder that could not be fully deleted, and to report it as an error if it remains
  • Improved the refusal for a path outside the working directories on macOS and Windows: when only its letter case differs from a path inside them, the message names that spelling
  • Improved the contrast of faint gray secondary text, such as hints, details in /stats, /model and /sandbox, and rejected-action messages
  • Improved the artifact database error when an update targets a document that does not exist, and when the service pauses repeated refused writes
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's warnings about a failed upstream call: each now names the upstream, not only its provider
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: it reads "spend limit reached · resets Dec 1", then admin.blocked_message if one is set
  • Improved the /model picker: older models are now grouped under a "More models" row instead of being listed after the current ones
  • Improved /context at the terminal so the table Claude reads stays short: each list keeps its 10 largest rows, and MCP tools that load on demand share one row per server until they're called
  • Improved /usage in cloud sessions: it now links to Settings → Usage on claude.ai in a case where plan limits can't be shown
  • [VSCode] Improved the confirmation for removing a plugin marketplace: it now checks which of its plugins are installed at that moment
  • Changed MCP tasks to work in the terminal without feature-flag fetching (Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, LLM gateways, DISABLE_TELEMETRY); set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASKS=1 to turn them off
  • Changed auto mode so that a project's settings files or a plugin can no longer switch its server-side check back on once you have switched it off outside the project
  • Changed Monitor's WebSocket watch to follow a rule on every Bash command: a deny refuses it, and under an ask rule an allow on Monitor, bypass mode or auto mode no longer skips the prompt
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS so that settings files can no longer set it where the host manages the network; set it in the process environment
  • Changed a session's exact Bash or PowerShell ask rule to be refused, not asked about, when a broader deny rule covers the command
  • Changed the Bash tool to ask for permission before running which with flags outside a lookup/display set
  • Changed --add-dir directories to register plugin marketplaces only once that directory's own trust dialog has been accepted
  • Changed nested skill loading: with the Bash sandbox on, skills in .claude/skills folders below the starting folder load only if you start Claude Code there or /cd there
  • Changed self-paced /loop to end when a turn finishes without rescheduling, instead of scheduling a fallback wakeup; set CLAUDE_CODE_LOOP_KEEPALIVE=1 to keep the old behavior
  • Changed PostToolUse hooks to run, with up to 10 seconds to finish, on tool calls that finish after a new message interrupts the turn
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a subagent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed cloud sessions to drop session-scoped allow rules at a move to a new worker when their deny and ask rules can't all be kept, so you may be asked again
  • Changed the automatic certificate repair behind a TLS-inspecting proxy: it no longer runs when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy variable set. Set HTTPS_PROXY to the proxy's http:// URL instead
  • Changed artifact database saves of rows others may have written: each file gets a hidden marker file, and existing files without one, earlier versions' exports among them, are left alone and reported
  • Updated /claude-api managed-agents-onboard templates to match the Claude Console: removed Performance tuner, renamed two, and turned off web search and fetch in five whose prompts don't use them
  • Removed shortcuts_list and shortcuts_execute, which listed and started shortcuts saved in the extension, from Claude Code's built-in Claude in Chrome tools
  • Gateway: Added startup warnings for upstreams that mix AWS GovCloud with other upstreams, and for base URL variables in the gateway's environment
  • Gateway: Added a start-up log warning when managed settings name an Amazon Bedrock guardrail in a header, which the gateway doesn't forward, and no bedrock upstream sets a guardrail
  • Gateway: Fixed Claude Desktop offering a web search tool that always failed when every upstream is Amazon Bedrock
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner started with --use-anthropic-git-proxy or --configure-git registering before a failed startup check made it exit; it now exits first
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_RUNNER_CHECKOUT_PATH so that each repository in a session gets its own folder: a folder name already taken in the session gets -2, -3, … at the end
  • Self-hosted runner: Removed the end-of-session upload of a session's debug log; a failed session's log stays on the runner host unless --remove-session-state is set
  • [VSCode] Fixed prompts over 50,000 characters being cut off silently: the prompt now stays in the chat box with a notice, and a paste over the limit is refused with a notice
  • [VSCode] Fixed a click on the survey or "Report a problem" buttons sending the unfinished prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed cloud sessions opened from the extension's Web tab bringing back turns that /clear, or Retry or Edit of a typed prompt, had removed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a deleted session's file coming back when that session was renamed in the extension
  • [VSCode] Fixed Claude carrying out an unapproved plan after a window reload: a step interrupted in plan mode now stops with a notice when the session comes back in another permission mode
  • [VSCode] Improved the "not signed in" message behind a Claude apps gateway: it now looks like an error and has a Sign in link
  • [VSCode] Changed links in Claude's replies that point at Claude sign-in, connector or API addresses to show as text with the address, instead of opening in the browser
  • [VSCode] Fixed a possible chat panel freeze when a dropped item's path contains a very long run of "/" characters
  • [VSCode] Fixed the claude-vscode.toggleDictation command starting dictation in every open Claude view at once; it now acts only in the view you are using, and a second press stops it
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat panel slowing down while a reply with many unclosed $$ math fences, each shorter than the last, streams in
  • [VSCode] Improved the chat panel's diagnostics tool for large workspaces: it leaves out files with no problems, returns compact JSON, and accepts an optional minimum severity
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed scheduled tasks silently dropping a connector named memory: runs now keep it, mounted under that name plus a short suffix
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Send now on a waiting message in cloud sessions ending running background agents; they now keep running
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the stalled-setup warning on self-hosted environments: its link now prefers your organization's default or an environment with a live runner, and names it
  • [Code Review] Changed unlinking a GitHub organization to also turn off its All repositories setting in Code Review; it stays off after you relink until you turn it back on
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag setup blocking launch when the channel list couldn't fully load; admins can now launch without picking a channel
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Claude Tag row to the Models admin page for Enterprise orgs with Claude Tag connected, linking to where its model defaults are managed
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed saving auto mode allow rules in Claude Tag admin settings overwriting another admin's changes; the save is now refused with a message
